title: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space
lede: Umberto Boccioni’s striding figure, whose muscles stream backward in flame-like planes, as if the body were shaped by the air it moves through.
summary: A bronze striding figure with flaring, wind-swept planes, on two blocks. Umberto Boccioni, 1913, bronze cast in the Museo del Novecento, Milan.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Umberto Boccioni Forme uniche nella continuità dello spazio 1913.jpg, photograph by Paolobon140

made: 1913 (plaster); the Milan bronze cast 1949 according to Wikipedia

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a photograph by the Commons user Paolobon140, 8 December 2015 (original 2912 × 4368 px; a 1067 × 1600 px rendering was inspected and stored). The file description says it shows the cast exhibited at the Museo del Novecento, Milan. Several casts exist; this record describes that cast. The photo has warm lighting, so the bronze color is not reliable.

styles.note: The movement’s best-known sculpture: a body in motion merged with the space around it, the three-dimensional form of lines of force.

context: The original plaster of 1913 is in the Museu de Arte Contemporânea da Universidade de São Paulo. Bronze casts were made in 1931 (one at MoMA), in 1949 (one at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and one at the Museo del Novecento, Milan), and in 1972 (Tate, and eight more cast from a 1949 bronze). The height is about 111 cm. [Wikipedia: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_Forms_of_Continuity_in_Space).
The sculpture is on the obverse of the Italian 20-cent euro coin. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_Forms_of_Continuity_in_Space).
observed: A headless or helmeted figure strides forward to the right, its rear leg stretched far back; each foot stands on its own rectangular block.
The calves and thighs flare backward into curved, blade-like fins, like flames or the wake of the motion.
The torso is made of hollow, overlapping curved planes; a short flat projection juts from the chest.
The surfaces are smooth and polished, with sharp edges where planes meet.
The photograph shows the sculpture on a white plinth against a plain warm wall.
interpretation: The figure does not show a body and then its trail; the trail is part of the body. This is the sculptural equivalent of Boccioni’s painted interpenetration of object and space in [Dynamism of a Cyclist](ref:boccioni-dynamism-of-a-cyclist-1913).
Its smooth, aerodynamic planes link it with the streamlined forms of later machine design.
borrow: Show speed by stretching the back edge of a form into trailing fins.
Let a form open into hollow planes so space passes through it.
Set a dynamic silhouette on two plain rectangular bases for contrast.

images.alt: Bronze sculpture of a striding figure on two rectangular blocks, against a plain warm wall. Its legs flare backward into curved fins like flames, and its torso is made of hollow overlapping planes.
images.caption: Umberto Boccioni, *Unique Forms of Continuity in Space*, 1913, bronze cast, Museo del Novecento, Milan. Photograph by Paolobon140, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Umberto_Boccioni_Forme_uniche_nella_continuit%C3%A0_dello_spazio_1913.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Photograph by Paolobon140, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons. Boccioni was Italian and died in 1916, so the sculpture is public domain in Italy. The plaster was exhibited in 1913. Because the work was already public domain in Italy on 1 January 1996, its US copyright was not restored under the URAA, so it is public domain in the United States even if the first casts of 1931 count as publication.
